product.body_html:
TOYS McCOY Men's Steve McQueen-Inspired Extra Heavyweight Raglan Pullover Hoodie, 14.8 oz Cotton Brushed-Back Fleece Hooded Sweatshirt, Tubular Body, Made in Japan TMC2542

TOYS McCOY

See available colors here.

This men's pullover hooded sweatshirt is made in Japan by TOYS McCOY and is inspired by the pullover hoodie worn by Steve McQueen in an off-duty photograph. Reinterpreted as a tribute to McQueen, it is made from 14.8 oz extra-heavyweight 100% cotton brushed-back sweatshirt fabric and incorporates a tubular side-seam-free body, raglan sleeves, a double-layer hood, a front kangaroo pocket, and extended rib-knit cuffs and waistband. Major joining areas, including the hood, shoulders, armholes, sleeves, cuffs, and waistband, are reinforced with parallel two-needle stitching. Together, these details create a substantial, classic athletic-sweatshirt character with a clean, understated appearance, while the relatively short body length and balanced regular fit make it easy to wear either on its own or layered under a jacket or coat.

Size and Fit Guide:

Gender: Men.

This hoodie has a balanced regular fit that is neither tight nor loose. The body is not cut excessively slim, nor does it have the exaggerated volume of an intentionally oversized silhouette. Instead, it provides moderate room through the body while keeping the overall length relatively short, creating a classic, compact shape. The raglan sleeve construction eliminates conventional shoulder seams, with the sleeves extending diagonally from the neckline to the underarms so they conform naturally around the shoulders. A relatively deep rib-knit waistband gently draws in the lower body around the waist, allowing the sweatshirt fabric to blouse slightly above the ribbing and create the softly rounded silhouette characteristic of classic sweat hoodies. The cuffs also use extended rib knit, which fits comfortably around the wrists and keeps the sleeve ends neatly in place. This balanced construction makes the hoodie easy to wear as a standalone sweatshirt while also allowing it to layer comfortably under jackets and coats.

Because fit may vary depending on body type and personal preference, please use the actual garment measurements below as your primary reference. For the most accurate comparison, we recommend measuring a similar hooded sweatshirt that fits you well. All measurements are taken by hand with a measuring tape, so slight variations may occur between individual garments and depending on the measuring method.

Our model wears Tagged Size M. He is 175 cm / approximately 5'9" tall, weighs 59 kg / approximately 130 lbs, and has a 91 cm / approximately 36" chest. For reference, he normally wears a US/EU size S/36.

1958 Steve McQueen Off-Screen Design Source
In 1958, Steve McQueen was photographed relaxing at his Laurel Canyon home, where he lived with his wife, Neile Adams. In the photograph, he wore a plain pullover sweatshirt hoodie with white jeans, creating a simple off-screen combination distinct from the costumes associated with his film roles.

This TOYS McCOY model takes that private moment and McQueen's understated pullover hoodie as its design source. Rather than relying on printed graphics or conspicuous decoration, the design is defined by the structure of the sweatshirt itself, including the extra-heavyweight cotton fabric, tubular body, raglan sleeves, double-layer hood, extended rib-knit components, kangaroo pocket, and visible double-needle stitching.

These elements reinterpret the atmosphere of McQueen's off-screen sweatshirt through TOYS McCOY's approach to vintage-inspired construction, producing a current pullover hoodie based on the proportions and functional details of classic American sweatwear.

14.8-Ounce Extra-Heavyweight 100% Cotton Sweatshirt Fabric
The sweatshirt is made from 14.8-ounce extra-heavyweight fabric knitted from 100% cotton. The material has substantial thickness, physical weight, and body, giving the garment a markedly heavier and more structured character than a lightweight or medium-weight sweatshirt.

The outer surface retains the rugged character of the yarns, with clearly visible vertical columns of knitted stitches. These vertically aligned columns, technically referred to as wales, are formed by successive knitted loops running along the length of the fabric. The wales remain visible across the surface and give the fabric an identifiable knitted structure rather than the flatter appearance of a woven textile.

The yarns and knitted loops also produce subtle natural variations in height, spacing, and surface texture. The fabric therefore does not appear completely smooth or mechanically uniform. Its slight irregularity and restrained surface variation create the straightforward, rugged appearance associated with traditional American sweatshirt fabrics.

The fabric has a firm body and a distinctly dry hand rather than an exceptionally soft, fluid, or loosely draped feel. Its substantial mass can also be felt when the garment is lifted or held in the hand. Together, the dry texture, firm resilience, visible knitted structure, and physical weight give the sweatshirt the substantial character expected from an extra-heavyweight fabric.

Brushed-Back Interior
The reverse side of the sweatshirt fabric is brushed to raise the cotton fibers and form a soft, finely napped interior surface. This differs from an unbrushed loopback sweatshirt fabric, where the looped yarn structure remains visibly exposed on the reverse side.

During brushing, fibers are lifted from the reverse surface without changing the fundamental knitted construction of the fabric. The resulting nap produces a softer interior texture while adding visible and tactile volume to the already substantial 14.8-ounce material.

Small spaces form among the raised fibers, allowing the brushed layer to hold pockets of air. When combined with the thickness and density of the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric, this structure helps retain warmth generated by the body.

Tubular Side-Seam-Free Body
The torso is knitted as a continuous tube on a circular knitting machine, creating what is commonly referred to as a tubular body. Unlike conventional cut-and-sewn construction, the body is not assembled from separate front and back panels joined along the left and right sides.

Because the torso forms one continuous knitted section, there are no vertical side seams along either side of the body. The corresponding seam allowances, folded edges, and overlapping layers of fabric that would normally occur at these locations are also eliminated.

Removing these side seams helps prevent localized thickness, hardness, and raised ridges from forming along the sides of the torso. This is particularly relevant with an extra-heavyweight fabric, where conventional stacked seam allowances could otherwise produce noticeable bulk. The uninterrupted tubular construction also gives the sweatshirt a clean side profile without visible vertical seam lines.

Tubular body construction is a traditional method found on vintage American T-shirts and sweatshirts. On this model, it forms an integral part of the garment's classic athletic-wear construction rather than serving as an applied decorative feature.

Unwashed Finish and Shrinkage Characteristics
The completed sweatshirt is supplied in an unwashed condition and has not undergone a final washing treatment during production. In its new state, the cotton fibers and knitted loops have not yet contracted and settled through exposure to water and drying. As a result, the spaces between the knitted loops may initially appear slightly more open.

During laundering, the cotton fibers absorb water and the knitted structure contracts naturally. As the garment dries, the loops settle closer together and the spacing between them becomes slightly tighter. This process can give the fabric a denser, more compact appearance and a firmer, more cohesive hand than it has in its original unwashed condition.

When the sweatshirt is gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and allowed to dry naturally in the shade, the resulting shrinkage tends to remain comparatively slight. Dimensional change is more likely to appear in the vertical direction, particularly in the body length, while the change across the body width tends to be smaller.

The exact amount and direction of shrinkage cannot be guaranteed. Results may vary according to the individual garment, water temperature, washing duration, mechanical agitation, spin intensity, reshaping after washing, and drying conditions.

Warm or hot water and tumble drying can cause the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract more extensively. These methods may produce greater and less predictable dimensional changes and should therefore be avoided.

Raglan Sleeve Construction
The sweatshirt uses raglan sleeves. Diagonal seams extend from the area near the neckline toward the underarms, joining each sleeve directly to the body.

This differs from set-in sleeve construction, where a shaped sleeve cap is attached to an armhole at the outer end of a defined shoulder seam. The raglan configuration eliminates a conventional shoulder seam positioned at a fixed shoulder point and creates a continuous transition from the neckline across the shoulder and into the upper arm.

Because the shoulder shape is not divided by a fixed horizontal shoulder seam, the sleeve and upper-body area can settle more naturally along the individual contours of the wearer's shoulders.

Double-Layer Hood Made from Matching Sweatshirt Fabric
The hood is constructed from two layers of the same sweatshirt fabric used for the body rather than as a single-layer component. Using the extra-heavyweight fabric on both the exterior and interior gives the hood substantial thickness, physical weight, and volume.

The double-layer structure supports the three-dimensional shape of the hood and helps prevent it from collapsing completely. When the hood is not worn over the head and rests against the upper back, it retains a fuller and more clearly defined outline than a lightweight single-layer hood.

Overlapping Hood Front with Buttonhole-Style Drawcord Openings
The front edges of the hood are not simply aligned edge to edge. Instead, one side overlaps the other at the front, creating a layered construction where the two sides meet near the neckline.

A pair of buttonhole-style openings is worked into the front of the hood to provide exit points for the drawcord. A flat drawcord passes through the hood channel and emerges through these two openings, allowing the circumference of the hood opening to be adjusted.

Because the hood front uses an overlapping construction, the two drawcord exit points may appear slightly asymmetrical when the garment is worn or viewed from the front. This visual difference results from the layered position of the hood edges and is a characteristic of the construction rather than a requirement for the openings to appear perfectly symmetrical.

Kangaroo Handwarmer Pocket
A kangaroo pocket made from the same sweatshirt fabric as the body is attached to the lower front. The pocket is constructed as a separate fabric panel laid over and sewn onto the exterior surface of the sweatshirt.

Openings on the left and right lead into one continuous interior compartment. Because the two sides are internally connected rather than divided into separate pockets, either hand can pass into the same central space from either opening.

The pocket is configured primarily as a handwarmer rather than as secure storage for small objects. Its large side openings provide easy access for both hands, but the continuous interior does not prevent stored items from moving toward and falling through either opening. Small valuables should therefore not be considered securely contained within the pocket.

Extended Double-Layer Rib-Knit Sleeve Cuffs
Each sleeve is finished with a separate rib-knit cuff. The rib-knit component is folded back on itself to form a double-layer structure and is then sewn to the end of the sweatshirt sleeve.

The rib knit has greater elasticity than the main sweatshirt fabric. This allows the cuff to follow the wrist with moderate tension while accommodating normal movement of the hand and arm. Its elasticity also helps prevent the sleeve opening from spreading excessively during wear.

The cuffs are proportionally longer than those used on many standard sweatshirts and cover a broader area around the wrists. This extended construction reduces open space at the sleeve ends through which cold air can enter while creating the distinctive long-cuff proportions associated with vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Extended Rib-Knit Waistband
The lower body is finished with a separate extended rib-knit waistband. Like the sleeve cuffs, the waistband has greater elasticity than the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric used for the body.

The rib knit follows the waist area with moderate tension and helps the lower edge of the sweatshirt settle around the waist rather than hanging freely below it. As the lower body is drawn inward by the waistband, a small amount of the substantial sweatshirt fabric gathers naturally above the ribbing.

This relationship between the full-bodied sweatshirt fabric and the more elastic waistband creates the softly rounded, cohesive silhouette associated with classic sweatshirt construction. The extended vertical depth of the ribbing also gives the lower body the longer waistband proportions characteristic of vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Double-Needle Stitching at Major Component Junctions
Double-needle stitching is used at major junctions throughout the sweatshirt, including the hood, raglan shoulder areas, armholes, sleeves, cuff attachments, and waistband attachment. Two parallel rows of stitching secure the joined components at these structural locations.

Using two rows of stitching broadens the secured area compared with a single stitched row. It also distributes tension across two parallel rows where the garment is repeatedly subjected to movement and pulling, helping stabilize the joined sections during normal wear.

The parallel rows remain visible on the exterior and make the functional seam construction part of the sweatshirt's appearance. Rather than serving as a separate decorative application, the visible stitching follows the actual component junctions and contributes to the straightforward sewing character associated with classic American sweatwear.

Decorative Label at the Front Left Hem
A decorative label is sewn onto the exterior of the front body near the left hem. Its localized placement creates a subtle visual focal point within the otherwise plain design, adding a restrained accent while preserving the clean overall appearance of the garment.

Care Instructions
Hand wash only. Do not machine wash.
Do not bleach.
Iron at a low temperature using a pressing cloth.
Do not dry clean.
Do not use a machine spin cycle. Drip dry in the shade.
Do not tumble dry.

Because this garment is made from unwashed 100% cotton sweatshirt fabric, washing allows the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract naturally. When gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and dried naturally in the shade, dimensional change tends to remain comparatively limited and may be more noticeable in the body-length direction than across the body. The actual degree and direction of shrinkage can vary according to water temperature, handling, drying conditions, and individual garment characteristics. Machine washing, warm or hot water, machine spin extraction, and tumble drying may cause greater and less predictable shrinkage and should be avoided.

Always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

product.title: Buzz Rickson's Men's Off-White Chambray Long-Sleeve Work Shirt, Modified 1950s U.S. Navy Utility Shirt Design, Made in Japan (BR25996 105 Ecru-Toned Off-White)
product.body_html:
Buzz Rickson's Men's Off-White Chambray Long-Sleeve Work Shirt, Modified 1950s U.S. Navy Utility Shirt Design, Made in Japan (BR25996 105 Ecru-Toned Off-White)

Buzz Rickson

This men's long-sleeve button-up shirt is made in Japan by Buzz Rickson's, Toyo Enterprise's military label specializing in vintage-inspired American military clothing. Its construction is based on the blue chambray utility shirts worn by U.S. Navy sailors during the 1950s, but the original blue chambray has been replaced with an ecru-toned off-white chambray, creating a distinctive Buzz Rickson's reinterpretation rather than an exact color reproduction. The lightweight 100% cotton chambray displays natural weave irregularities, small neps, and subtle, linen-like wrinkling, giving the fabric a rough, rustic workwear character. The shirt incorporates period-inspired details such as a collar stand, flapless buttoned chest pockets, rounded shirttail hem, selvedge side gussets, and chain-stitch runoffs extending from the side seams at the hem. Together, these details preserve the practical character of the original design while giving the shirt a lighter, more understated appearance. Its balanced silhouette is neither overly slim nor excessively loose, allowing it to blend naturally into contemporary casual wardrobes.

Size and Fit Guide:

Gender: Men.

This shirt has a balanced silhouette that is neither overly slim nor excessively loose and falls broadly within the range of a regular fit. The shoulders and body are not cut especially narrow, nor does the shirt have the added volume of an intentionally oversized design. The body is not heavily tapered from the chest to the hem, allowing it to fall in a relatively straight, natural line. The front and back are finished with a gently rounded shirttail hem, making the shirt suitable for wearing either tucked in or untucked. Made from relatively lightweight chambray, it can be worn on its own or open over a T-shirt or other lightweight top. The fabric is also light enough to layer easily under a jacket or other outerwear.

Because fit may vary depending on body type and personal preference, please use the actual garment measurements below as your primary reference. For the most accurate comparison, we recommend measuring a similar long-sleeve shirt that fits you well. All measurements are taken by hand with a measuring tape, so slight variations may occur from one garment to another and depending on the measuring method.

Lightweight 100% Cotton Ecru-Toned Off-White Chambray Fabric
The shirt is made from lightweight 100% cotton chambray fabric. Off-white yarns are used in both the lengthwise warp and crosswise weft, creating a unified ecru-toned appearance across the fabric.

Conventional blue chambray generally combines blue warp yarns with white weft yarns, producing a blue-toned, heathered appearance as the two yarn colors intersect. On this shirt, the use of off-white yarns in both directions creates a more consistent natural color while preserving the fine woven texture and subtle shading characteristic of chambray. The result is brighter than conventional blue chambray but remains subdued rather than appearing stark or uniformly white.

Natural Weave Variation, Neps, and Linen-Like Wrinkling
The fabric retains the natural character of the yarns, with slight weave irregularities, fine surface undulation, and small variations in texture visible throughout. Rather than forming a completely flat and mechanically uniform surface, the intersecting yarns create subtle differences in height, tension, and shading.

Fine brown and nearly black flecks originating from the natural cotton are scattered throughout the ecru-colored yarns. Small neps also appear intermittently where irregular or slightly thicker sections of yarn rise above the surrounding weave. These details give the fabric visible depth at close range without forming a printed or intentionally patterned surface.

Although the fabric is made entirely from cotton, it also develops natural creasing and subtle surface wrinkling that can recall the appearance of linen. The combination of woven irregularity, cotton-derived flecks, small neps, and linen-like wrinkles gives the cloth a rustic and slightly rough workwear character rather than the smooth appearance of a highly uniform shirting fabric.

These characteristics are not stains or fabric defects. They are inherent features of the natural ecru cotton yarns and the woven structure of the chambray. Their placement, size, and concentration may vary slightly between different areas of the fabric and from one garment to another.

Lightweight Fabric with Moderate Firmness and Resilience
The chambray is thin and lightweight, but it is not exceptionally soft, fluid, or strongly draped. The fabric retains moderate firmness, crispness, and resilience, giving it enough body to support the outline of a traditional work shirt.<
Boundary>

It does not have the weight or volume of a heavy work-shirt fabric, yet its remaining structure prevents it from collapsing closely against the body like a softer and more fluid shirting material. This balance allows the shirt to remain lightweight while preserving a clearly defined workwear shape.

With repeated wear and laundering, the initial firmness gradually relaxes. The cotton fabric becomes progressively more pliable and conforms more naturally to the wearer while retaining the woven character of the chambray.

One-Wash Finish
The completed shirt is given a one-wash finish during the final production stage. Washing the garment before sale relaxes part of the fabric's initial rigidity, so the chambray feels less hard at the beginning of wear than it would in a completely unwashed state. The process does not eliminate the moderate firmness and body that define the fabric.

Because the garment has already been washed once during production, the possibility of substantial initial shrinkage after purchase is reduced to some extent compared with an untreated, unwashed cotton shirt. However, the fabric is not shrink-proof. Slight additional dimensional changes may still occur depending on the washing method, water temperature, drying conditions, frequency of laundering, and individual garment variation.

Changes with Wear and Laundering
With continued wear and washing, the cotton chambray gradually becomes more pliable, while the natural creasing and definition of the weave become increasingly pronounced. The fabric therefore develops from its original new-garment condition into a surface and hand that conform more naturally to the wearer.

Fine puckering and subtle wear-related shading may also develop around the seams. As the fabric contracts and relaxes around the stitched areas, the differences in height and shadow between the chambray and sewing lines become more visible, gradually giving the construction greater dimensional definition.

Because the fabric is ecru-toned off-white, its development differs from the obvious fading normally associated with dark dyed cloth. Changes appear primarily through increased pliability, deeper woven texture, more defined wrinkles, and subtle shadows around the seams. These characteristics allow the off-white chambray to develop its own distinctive appearance through continued wear and laundering.

Point Collar with a Separate Collar Stand
The neckline is finished with a standard point collar attached to a separate collar stand. The collar narrows naturally toward the points, creating the familiar profile of a traditional button-front work shirt.

The separate stand forms a supporting band around the base of the neck. This construction stabilizes the collar body and gives the neckline moderate dimensional definition instead of allowing the collar to lie completely flat against the upper body.

Unlike a camp collar or open collar designed primarily to remain spread at the neckline, this collar can be fastened completely with the top button. When fully buttoned, the collar maintains a more orderly and defined shape. When the top button is left open, it forms a natural opening around the neck for more casual wear.

Full Six-Button Front with Asymmetrical Placket Construction
The shirt uses a full-opening button front that extends from the neckline to the hem. Six buttons are arranged along the front, and the corresponding buttonholes are oriented vertically in line with the opening. This configuration allows the garment to be opened completely for dressing and removal.

The two sides of the front opening use different construction methods. On the left front panel, a separate strip of matching chambray is folded to form a double layer and sewn onto the body as an applied placket. The added layer reinforces the buttonhole side and gives the front edge a stable, clearly defined shape.

On the right front panel, the edge of the body fabric is turned inward to create a doubled integrated facing rather than using a separate applied placket component. This folded section supports the button attachments and reinforces the opposite front edge.

Together, the applied placket and integrated facing reinforce both sides of the opening while preserving the asymmetrical front construction found on traditional work shirts.

Flapless Buttoned Chest Patch Pockets
Two patch pockets are sewn directly onto the exterior of the chest. The pockets do not use separate flaps. Instead, the upper edge of each pocket body is turned inward to form a double-layer opening.

The doubled upper section reinforces the part of the pocket that is repeatedly handled when items are inserted or removed. A buttonhole is worked into this reinforced section, and the pocket opening is secured by a button sewn to the shirt body behind it.

This construction closes the pocket directly without adding the separate layer and visual weight of an independent pocket flap. Both lower corners of each pocket are formed with gentle curves rather than sharp points. The rounded shape softens the outline of the pockets while retaining the direct and functional construction of a traditional work shirt.

Long Set-In Sleeve Construction
The shirt uses conventional long set-in sleeves. Each shaped sleeve cap is sewn into the corresponding armhole, with the sleeve beginning at the outer end of the shoulder seam. This establishes a clearly defined boundary between the body and sleeve and allows the sleeve to fall naturally from the shoulder along the arm.

This differs from raglan construction, in which the sleeve panel extends diagonally toward the neckline. The set-in configuration uses distinct shoulder and sleeve pattern sections, supporting the traditional shoulder shape and orderly appearance associated with a classic button-front work shirt.

Square Single-Button Cuffs and Sleeve Slits
Each sleeve is finished with a single-button cuff. The cuff ends have straight, square corners rather than rounded edges, reinforcing the shirt's simple and functional workwear appearance.

The cuff buttonhole is positioned horizontally in relation to the sleeve opening. This orientation corresponds to the lateral tension placed on the closure when the cuff is fastened around the wrist and helps the buttonhole receive that force along its length.

A slit opening is incorporated above each cuff. When the cuff button is released, the slit allows the lower sleeve to spread wider so the hand can pass through more easily. The opening also makes it easier to turn back the lower sleeve when the shirt is worn with the cuffs rolled.

Off-White Urea Two-Hole Dish-Shaped Buttons
Off-white two-hole buttons made from urea resin are used at the front, chest pockets, and cuffs. Each button has a dimensional dish-shaped profile with a recessed center. This recess allows the attachment thread to sit within the center of the button rather than protruding prominently above its surface.

Positioning the thread within the recessed area reduces its direct exposure to surface friction and accidental snagging while helping keep the thread centered and stable. This is a functional button construction rather than a purely decorative shape.

The off-white buttons and sewing thread are coordinated with the ecru-toned chambray. This tonal combination gives the shirt a unified appearance without concealing the practical construction of the individual components.

Double-Layer Back Yoke
The upper back is divided by a yoke panel extending across both shoulders. The back yoke is constructed from two layers of matching chambray, adding reinforcement to the shoulder and upper-back area where the shirt is repeatedly subjected to tension during dressing and arm movement.

The doubled construction also adds localized thickness and stability to the upper back. It supports the surrounding seams and helps the shoulder area retain its defined structure through repeated wear and laundering while the remainder of the shirt maintains the lighter character of the single-layer chambray.

Clean Back Construction Without Pleats
The back does not include pleats or decorative paneling below the yoke. Instead, the body falls directly and naturally from the lower edge of the back yoke toward the hem, creating a straightforward and uncluttered construction.

The double-layer yoke supplies reinforcement across the shoulders, while the uninterrupted lower back allows the lightweight chambray to retain its natural flexibility. The broad fabric surface also displays the ecru tone, fine weave, intermittent neps, and naturally wrinkled texture without additional seams or decorative interruptions.

Rounded Shirttail Hem
The hem is cut in a rounded shirttail shape. On both the front and back, the hem curves upward from the center toward the side seams. This is a traditional hem profile commonly associated with classic work shirts.

When the shirt is worn untucked, the front and back curves avoid the straight, flat horizontal line created by a square-cut hem. Instead, the rounded sections follow the body and fall in a softer, more natural line around the waist and hips.

Selvedge Triangular Side Gussets
A small triangular gusset is installed where each side seam meets the hem. This junction is particularly vulnerable to concentrated stress because body movement and pulling across the lower shirt place repeated tension on the terminal point of the side seam.

Adding a separate reinforcing piece helps distribute this tension over a broader area and reduces direct strain on the seam end and hem edge. The gussets therefore help protect the lower side seams from splitting or fraying. This is a functional reinforcement method found on older work shirts rather than a purely decorative addition.

Each gusset uses the selvedge edge of the chambray. The selvedge is the finished outer edge formed during the weaving of the fabric. It is not displayed prominently across the shirt and can be seen only within these small reinforcement pieces at the side hems.

This restrained use of the fabric edge provides a subtle indication of the cloth's woven construction and recalls manufacturing details associated with older workwear. It does not serve as a large exterior decoration.

Two-Row Chain-Stitch Runoffs at the Side Hems
Two chain-stitch runoff tails are deliberately left extending from the lower side seams. A runoff is formed when a chain-stitch sewing machine continues feeding thread after the completed seam has passed beyond the edge of the fabric. With no fabric between the stitches, the interlocking thread loops continue as narrow chains.

These tails are not separate strands twisted together and attached to the hem. They are direct continuations of the chain stitching used to construct the side seams. Leaving the runoffs untrimmed reproduces a sewing detail associated with vintage work shirts and older garment-production methods.

Because the runoffs hang freely from the side hems, their length, direction, and the way the thread chains gather may vary slightly from one garment to another. This variation is normal. The visible thread chains are not evidence of loose sewing, an unfinished seam, or a missed trimming operation. They are an intentional construction detail.

Double-Needle Felled Seam Construction
Double-needle felled seams are used at major structural areas, including the side seams, shoulder seams, armholes, back yoke, and sleeves. These locations are regularly subjected to movement, pulling, and repeated stress during wear.

In this construction, the raw fabric edges and seam allowances are folded and enclosed within the seam rather than being left exposed. Two parallel rows of stitching secure the folded layers. Enclosing the cut edges helps control fraying, keeps the seam allowances stable, and reinforces the joined fabric panels.

The two stitch rows secure a broader section of fabric than a single row and help distribute stress along the length of the seam. This is particularly relevant at the armholes and side seams, where repeated arm and body movement continually places tension on the construction.

The parallel stitch lines remain visible on the exterior, making the structural construction of the shirt part of its appearance. With repeated wear and laundering, fine puckering and subtle wear marks may develop around these seams, gradually increasing the dimensional relationship between the stitching and chambray.

Interior Buzz Rickson & Co. Woven Label
A Buzz Rickson & Co. woven label is attached inside the collar. No large brand logo or decorative branding is applied to the exterior. The identifying brand element is kept inside the garment, preserving the restrained appearance of the shirt.

Made in Japan
This shirt is made in Japan by Buzz Rickson's. It combines lightweight 100% cotton off-white chambray with a point collar and separate collar stand, asymmetrical front placket construction, flapless buttoned chest pockets, long set-in sleeves, square single-button cuffs, a double-layer back yoke, a rounded shirttail hem, selvedge side gussets, chain-stitch runoffs, and double-needle felled seams.

The construction retains the practical details associated with a 1950s U.S. Navy utility shirt while replacing the conventional blue chambray with ecru-toned off-white cloth. The result is a Buzz Rickson's original reinterpretation that combines vintage workwear construction with the brand's own off-white color treatment.

Model: Buzz Rickson's by Toyo Enterprises / Lot No. BR25996 / White Chambray Work Shirt (Long Sleeve).


Care Instructions
Machine wash at a maximum temperature of 30°C / 86°F using a very gentle cycle.
Do not bleach.
Do not tumble dry.
Line dry in the shade.
Iron at a low temperature with a pressing cloth placed between the iron and garment.
Gentle dry cleaning with petroleum-based solvents is permitted.
Gentle professional wet cleaning is permitted.

Because this is a cotton garment, slight additional shrinkage may occur depending on the washing method, water temperature, and drying conditions, even though the shirt has already received a one-wash finish.

Always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

Overall Product Character
These men's brown denim jeans are made in Japan by Studio D'Artisan and combine the construction of classic five-pocket jeans with two distinctive Japanese production techniques: low-speed denim weaving on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom and traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The jeans are constructed from substantial 15 oz. cotton denim woven from undyed ecru warp and weft yarns. After the denim is cut and sewn into jeans, the completed garment is dyed on Amami Oshima using a repeated botanical-dyeing and mud-treatment process. This creates a deep, earthy brown color with natural variations in tone.

The irregular surface of the GL-3-woven denim contains visible neps, uneven yarn thickness, fine raised cotton fibers that create a subtly fuzzy surface, and irregular variations in texture. These characteristics are combined with the naturally developed brown coloration of Amami Dorozome to create a fabric that differs in both appearance and feel from conventional indigo denim.

The design follows the traditional structure of five-pocket jeans, including a button fly, curved front hand pockets, a coin pocket, rear patch pockets, metal rivets, five belt loops, and a leather brand patch. The result is a practical pair of everyday jeans with a distinctive fabric texture and naturally developed brown color.

Silhouette and Fit
These jeans have a classic regular straight fit with a standard mid rise. The silhouette is neither excessively loose nor closely tapered.

The upper legs provide moderate room through the thighs, allowing comfortable movement without creating an oversized appearance. From the knees to the leg openings, the legs narrow very slightly while maintaining the natural line of traditional straight-leg jeans.

The balanced proportions preserve the substantial appearance associated with classic workwear while remaining easy to coordinate with contemporary casual clothing. The regular straight shape can be worn with boots, sneakers, or other everyday footwear without appearing strongly influenced by short-term fashion trends.

15 oz. GL-3 Loom-Woven Denim
The jeans are made from 15 oz. denim woven from 100% cotton yarn on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom. The GL-3 was manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation, during the 1950s and is considered one of Japan's early motorized power looms.

Unlike modern high-speed textile machinery, the GL-3 operates at an extremely low production rate. It can weave only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This slow weaving speed allows the yarns to retain more of their natural irregularity and prevents the fabric from becoming excessively compressed, flat, or mechanically uniform.

The resulting denim has a substantial hand and a visibly irregular surface. Variations in yarn thickness and placement create neps, rough areas, uneven elevations, and fine raised cotton fibers that give the fabric a slightly fuzzy surface appearance.

The combination of surface fuzz, neps, irregular yarn thickness, and rough texture gives the denim a dry, rugged, and three-dimensional character that is different from the smooth and uniform surface of conventionally manufactured denim.

These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They are inherent features of denim produced from irregular yarns on early low-speed weaving equipment.

Studio D'Artisan Original Denim Specification
The denim was developed according to Studio D'Artisan's original fabric specification. The yarn count, yarn shape, warp and weft density, number of inserted yarns, and weaving conditions were selected to emphasize the distinctive characteristics of the GL-3 loom.

The interaction between the irregular cotton yarns and the low-speed weaving process produces a surface that is not uniformly smooth. Small neps, uneven yarn thickness, fine raised cotton fibers, and irregular variations in texture may be visible throughout the garment.

The fine cotton fibers extending from the surface create a subtle degree of fuzziness. This surface character is a natural result of the yarn and weaving specifications and should not be confused with pilling or fabric damage.

The substantial 15 oz. weight gives the jeans a firm structure, while the irregular texture and fine surface fuzz create a three-dimensional appearance that becomes more noticeable under changing light and through continued wear.

Undyed Ecru Warp and Weft Yarns
Both the warp and weft yarns are initially undyed ecru cotton. This differs from conventional blue denim, which is normally woven with indigo-dyed warp yarns and undyed weft yarns.

These jeans are not made by taking conventional indigo denim and redyeing it brown. Instead, the GL-3 denim is woven entirely from undyed yarns before the completed garment is treated with Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

Beginning with an undyed denim base allows the natural dye to penetrate both the warp and weft yarns. This produces a brown color throughout the structure of the cloth while preserving the neps, fine surface fuzz, uneven elevations, and rough texture created during weaving.

Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyeing Process
The jeans are dyed using Amami Dorozome, a traditional natural dyeing method practiced on Amami Oshima, an island in southern Japan.

The process uses a botanical dye extracted from the locally grown Techi tree, known in Japanese as Sharinbai. Its botanical classification is Rhaphiolepis indica var. umbellata. The wood and bark of the tree contain natural tannins that can penetrate cotton fibers and react with iron.

The garment is repeatedly immersed in the plant-based dye solution so that the tannins can gradually enter the cotton fibers. It is then immersed in iron-rich mud from Amami Oshima.

The iron contained in the mud reacts with the tannins absorbed into the fabric. This natural chemical reaction darkens the material and helps fix the color within the cotton fibers. Repeated botanical-dyeing and mud-treatment cycles gradually build the deep, earthy brown tone.

The process requires considerable time and repeated manual work. Because the final color is created through the interaction of plant-derived tannins, iron-rich mud, water, cotton yarn, and individual processing conditions, the resulting shade is not mechanically uniform.

Minor differences in color depth, surface tone, and dye concentration may occur between individual pairs and between different areas of the same garment. These variations are inherent characteristics of traditional natural dyeing and should not be regarded as defects.

Garment-Dyed Construction
The jeans are dyed after the denim has been cut and sewn into a completed garment. This garment-dyeing method allows the Amami Dorozome color to develop across the main fabric, seams, pocket edges, belt loops, reinforced areas, and other structural details.

Because areas containing multiple layers of denim may absorb and retain the dye differently from single-layer areas, subtle tonal differences may appear around the seams, pockets, waistband, fly, and hems.

The neps, raised cotton fibers, rough areas, and uneven elevations of the GL-3 denim may also absorb and reflect the color differently. This interaction between the irregular fabric surface and the natural dye contributes to the depth and variation of the finished brown color.

These small differences contribute to the natural appearance of the finished jeans and reflect the interaction between the garment's construction, the GL-3-woven denim, and the traditional dyeing process.

One-Wash Finish
The finished jeans have been washed once before sale. This one-wash treatment removes a portion of the initial shrinkage and softens the rigid feel of newly woven 15 oz. denim, allowing the jeans to feel more comfortable and easier to wear from the beginning.

Although the one-wash process reduces initial shrinkage, minor additional shrinkage or dimensional change may still occur depending on water temperature, washing method, drying conditions, and frequency of laundering.

The fabric may also stretch slightly in areas exposed to repeated movement and pressure, particularly around the waist, seat, knees, and thighs. This combination of minor shrinkage and wear-related stretching is a normal characteristic of cotton denim.

Wear and Color Development
The mud-dyed brown surface will gradually change through repeated wear, friction, movement, and washing. Areas exposed to frequent abrasion, including the pocket openings, fly edges, knees, thighs, seams, hems, and rear pocket edges, may gradually develop lighter tones and more visible surface contrast.

The fine raised fibers on the surface may gradually settle, flatten, or wear away in areas exposed to repeated friction. At the same time, recessed sections may retain more of their original fuzziness and darker color. This difference can make the irregular elevations, neps, and three-dimensional texture of the GL-3 denim increasingly visible.

The resulting color and texture development will vary according to the wearer's body shape, movement, frequency of wear, washing method, drying conditions, and daily use. No two pairs will develop exactly the same appearance.

Because natural dyeing does not produce the same perfectly uniform and highly colorfast surface associated with some modern synthetic dye systems, gradual fading, tonal variation, and occasional color transfer should be regarded as inherent characteristics of the jeans.

Five-Button Button Fly
The front opening uses a traditional button-fly construction. It consists of one top button at the waistband and four buttons along the fly, for a total of five buttons.

The buttons are made from metal and finished with a black coating that coordinates with the earthy brown denim. Each button is stamped with the Studio D'Artisan brand logo.

The button fly reinforces the classic five-pocket construction and provides a more traditional appearance than a zipper fly. With extended use, friction may gradually alter the black coating on the raised edges of the buttons. This surface change is a natural result of wear.

Curved Front Hand Pockets
Curved hand pockets are positioned on the left and right sides of the front body. The openings are shaped to provide practical access while maintaining the familiar appearance of classic five-pocket jeans.

Metal rivets reinforce the ends of the pocket openings. These areas receive concentrated stress when the wearer inserts a hand or carries an object inside the pocket. The rivets help distribute this stress and reduce the possibility of the pocket corners separating from the surrounding denim.

The pocket openings and riveted corners may gradually develop lighter color and more pronounced surface contrast through repeated use.

Coin Pocket
A coin pocket is incorporated into the right front pocket area. It follows the compact construction traditionally used on classic five-pocket jeans.

The coin pocket is also reinforced with metal rivets at stress points. Although originally intended for carrying small items, it also serves as a recognizable structural and visual detail associated with traditional jeans.

Rear Patch Pockets and Hidden Rivets
Two patch pockets are positioned on the back, one on each side. They are constructed from the same 15 oz. Amami Dorozome mud-dyed denim as the main body.

The upper corners of the rear pockets are reinforced with hidden rivets installed inside the pocket construction. These rivets strengthen the high-stress attachment points while remaining concealed from the exterior.

This construction preserves a clean outer appearance while providing reinforcement similar to the exposed rivets used on the front pockets.

Signature Back-Pocket Stitching
Both rear pockets feature Studio D'Artisan's original decorative stitching pattern. The stitching is applied in a brown-toned thread selected to coordinate with the mud-dyed fabric.

The restrained color reduces strong contrast and allows the stitching to remain integrated with the overall earthy appearance of the jeans.

As the surrounding denim changes through wear and washing, the relationship between the pocket stitching and the fabric color may gradually become more visible.

Five Belt Loops
The waistband is equipped with five belt loops positioned around the waist. This traditional arrangement provides practical support for a belt while maintaining the balanced construction of classic five-pocket jeans.

The belt loops are made from the same mud-dyed denim. Their raised edges and areas of contact with a belt may develop lighter color and surface wear over time.

Leather Brand Patch
A Studio D'Artisan leather brand patch is sewn onto the right rear section of the waistband. The patch identifies the brand while adding a natural material that will change through continued wear.

The leather may gradually soften and develop changes in color and surface texture through exposure to friction, moisture, body heat, and daily use.

Natural differences in grain, tone, and texture may be visible in the leather. These variations are inherent characteristics of the material rather than defects.

Classic Five-Pocket Construction
The jeans follow the basic structure of traditional five-pocket workwear, including two curved front hand pockets, one coin pocket, two rear patch pockets, riveted stress points, a button fly, five belt loops, and a rear leather patch.

Rather than serving as a reproduction of one specific historical model, the design combines these established jeans details with Studio D'Artisan's original 15 oz. GL-3 denim and the natural coloration of Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The result is a regular straight pair of jeans that retains the practical structure of traditional workwear while presenting a naturally developed brown color, fine surface fuzz, and irregular texture created through specialized Japanese weaving and dyeing processes.

Natural-Dye Color Transfer
These jeans are colored with natural dye. Excess dye remaining on or near the fabric surface may transfer to other materials through friction.

Particular care should be taken during the initial period of wear. Avoid combining the jeans with white or light-colored clothing, bags, shoes, belts, furniture, automobile seats, upholstery, or other items that may easily absorb pigment.

Color transfer may occur while the jeans are dry, but the risk increases when the fabric is damp from perspiration, rain, washing, or high humidity. Areas exposed to repeated friction may also release color more readily.

Do not place the wet or damp jeans directly against other clothing or household surfaces. Do not leave the garment folded, compressed, or in contact with another item while wet, as dissolved dye may migrate and create staining.

Washing and Care Precautions
Wash these jeans separately from other garments because released dye may transfer during washing.

Turn the jeans inside out before washing to reduce direct abrasion against the dyed outer surface. Use cold or lukewarm water, a mild detergent, and a gentle washing cycle. Avoid excessive agitation, scrubbing, brushing, or concentrated rubbing.

Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach. Avoid hot water and tumble drying. Do not leave the jeans soaking for an extended period, as prolonged immersion may cause excessive dye loss or uneven color migration.

After washing, remove the jeans promptly, reshape them carefully, and allow them to air-dry naturally in the shade. Do not leave the garment wet or folded for an extended period.

Because of the natural dyeing process, some color loss is expected during washing. Variations in fading and surface tone are part of the intended character of the garment.

Always follow the specific care instructions attached to the product.

Made in Japan
These jeans are made in Japan from Studio D'Artisan's original 15 oz. cotton denim woven on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom and colored using traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The irregular fabric surface, fine cotton fuzz, natural coloration, hardware, five-pocket construction, and regular straight silhouette combine specialized Japanese textile production with the practical design principles of classic jeans.


Toyoda GL-3 Power Loom

An Early Japanese Power Loom
The GL-3 is an early Japanese shuttle-type power loom manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation. It was produced during the 1950s and represents an early stage in the development of motorized weaving technology in Japan.

Only a limited number of GL-3 looms were manufactured, and very few remain operational today. Their rarity, low production capacity, and distinctive weaving characteristics have made them highly valued for producing specialized fabrics with pronounced surface variation.

Difficult to Maintain
Replacement parts for the GL-3 are no longer commercially manufactured. When a component becomes worn or damaged, usable parts may need to be recovered from another retired or non-operational GL-3 loom.

Keeping the machine in working condition requires experienced technicians who understand its mechanical timing, shuttle movement, yarn tension, take-up system, and other operating characteristics.

Small changes in alignment or mechanical adjustment can affect both the stability of the weaving process and the appearance of the finished fabric. Regular inspection, careful adjustment, and continued maintenance are therefore essential.

Extremely Slow Weaving Speed
A GL-3 can weave only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This is considerably slower than contemporary high-speed looms designed for large-scale industrial production.

From a manufacturing perspective, the GL-3 is highly inefficient. It requires more time, closer supervision, and greater mechanical attention to produce a relatively small quantity of fabric.

However, the slow operating speed allows the yarns to be woven without creating the highly compressed, smooth, and mechanically uniform surface commonly associated with modern mass-produced textiles.

Why the GL-3 Is Called a "Phantom Loom"
The GL-3 is sometimes referred to as a "phantom loom" because very few operational machines remain, replacement parts are difficult to obtain, and the technical knowledge required to maintain them is increasingly specialized.

The term also refers to the distinctive fabric character produced by the machine. Depending on the yarn and weaving specifications, the GL-3 can produce visible neps, slubs, uneven elevations, fine surface fuzz, and subtle variations in surface density that are difficult to reproduce with modern high-speed equipment.

These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They result from the combination of irregular yarns, low-speed weaving, carefully controlled tension, and the mechanical properties of the older loom.

Fabric Characteristics Produced by the GL-3
Fabric woven on the GL-3 typically has a substantial hand and a visibly irregular surface. Differences in yarn thickness, tension, and placement create raised and recessed areas throughout the cloth.

Small neps, slubs, fine raised cotton fibers, and irregular variations in texture may be visible. Neps are small groups of entangled fibers, while slubs are thicker sections formed within intentionally irregular yarns.

The fine cotton fibers extending from the surface give the fabric a subtly fuzzy appearance and tactile texture. This natural surface fuzz is distinct from pilling and is an intended characteristic of the denim.

Rather than appearing perfectly flat and uniform, the surface contains subtle variations that become more noticeable under changing light and through continued use.

The exact appearance and hand of the fabric depend on the yarn count, yarn irregularity, warp density, weft density, weaving tension, and other production specifications selected for each fabric.

Craftsmanship Rather Than Production Efficiency
Producing fabric on the GL-3 requires substantially more time and manual involvement than weaving on modern industrial machinery.

The loom must be carefully maintained, weaving conditions must be monitored, and mechanical adjustments may be required during production. The objective is not maximum output or complete visual uniformity, but the creation of fabric with controlled irregularity and distinctive surface character.

Each length of fabric reflects the interaction between the loom, the yarn specification, the mechanical settings, and the judgment of the loom operator.

The GL-3 therefore represents a production method that prioritizes fabric character, technical skill, and careful small-scale manufacturing over speed and efficiency.

Handling Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyed Products

Traditional Amami Dorozome Dyeing
Amami Dorozome is a traditional mud-dyeing method practiced on Amami Oshima in southern Japan.

The process uses a botanical dye extracted from the Techi tree, also known in Japanese as Sharinbai. The wood and bark contain natural tannins that can bond with textile fibers and react with iron.

The material is repeatedly immersed in the plant-based dye solution so that the tannins penetrate the fibers. It is then treated with iron-rich mud from Amami Oshima.

The iron in the mud reacts with the tannins and gradually deepens and fixes the color. Multiple dyeing and mud-treatment cycles are required to build the characteristic earthy tone.

Natural Color Variation
Amami Dorozome does not produce the mechanically uniform appearance associated with conventional synthetic dyeing.

Minor differences in color depth, concentration, and surface tone may occur between individual products. Subtle variations may also be visible within different areas of the same product.

Seams, folds, reinforced areas, and sections containing multiple layers of fabric may absorb or retain the dye differently from single-layer areas.

These variations are inherent characteristics of the traditional dyeing process and should not be regarded as defects.

Color Transfer Through Friction
Natural dye remaining on or near the surface may transfer to other materials through friction.

Particular care should be taken when a mud-dyed product comes into contact with white or light-colored clothing, bags, shoes, furniture, automobile seats, upholstery, or other finished surfaces.

Areas exposed to repeated rubbing may release color more readily. Color transfer is often more noticeable during the early period of use, although it may continue depending on moisture, friction, and washing conditions.

Color Transfer When Wet or Damp
Moisture can increase the possibility of dye transfer. Perspiration, rain, washing water, humidity, or other sources of moisture may cause the surface dye to become more mobile.

When the product is damp, avoid direct contact with light-colored clothing, bags, furniture, automobile seats, and other materials that may absorb the dye.

Do not leave the wet product folded, compressed, or placed against another item for an extended period. Prolonged contact while wet may result in color transfer, uneven staining, or migration of dye between different sections.

Washing Instructions
Wash mud-dyed products separately from other items because released dye may transfer during washing.

When appropriate for the product, turn it inside out before washing. This reduces direct abrasion against the dyed outer surface and may help limit unnecessary surface color loss.

Use cold or lukewarm water, a mild detergent, and a gentle washing method. Avoid excessive mechanical agitation, scrubbing, brushing, or concentrated rubbing.

Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach. Avoid hot water and tumble drying unless specifically permitted by the care label attached to the product.

After washing, remove the product promptly, reshape it carefully, and allow it to air-dry naturally in the shade. Do not leave it soaking or wet for an extended period.

Always follow the specific care instructions provided on the product label.

Drying and Sunlight Precautions
When appropriate, turn the product inside out before drying and place it in a well-ventilated shaded area.

Avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight. Strong ultraviolet light may cause natural dyes to fade, discolor, or change unevenly, particularly when the product remains exposed in the same position for an extended period.

Direct sunlight should not be used intentionally to darken or develop the color, as it may instead cause unwanted or uneven fading.

Natural Aging and Color Development
The color and surface appearance of Amami Dorozome products will gradually change through use, friction, washing, moisture, and exposure to air.

Areas that receive frequent contact may become lighter, while recessed or less exposed areas may retain a darker tone. The resulting appearance will vary according to how the product is used, cleaned, dried, and stored.

No two naturally dyed products will develop in exactly the same manner.

Characteristics of Natural Dye
Color fading, surface variation, and occasional color transfer are inherent characteristics of Amami Dorozome and other natural dyeing methods.

These properties differ from the high degree of color uniformity and colorfastness commonly associated with modern synthetic dyes.

Careful handling can reduce unwanted transfer and uneven fading, but it cannot completely prevent the natural color from changing over time.

Please handle Amami Dorozome products with appropriate care and enjoy the individual color development and surface character created through continued use.

Care Instructions
Machine wash on a gentle cycle at a maximum water temperature of 40°C (104°F).
Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach.
Iron at a medium temperature with a pressing cloth placed between the iron and the garment.
Do not dry clean.
Due to the nature of the dye, color loss may occur. Wash separately from other garments.
Due to the characteristics of the fabric, slight shrinkage may occur after washing.
Color may transfer to other clothing, accessories, upholstery, or other surfaces through friction or when the garment is damp from perspiration, rain, or other moisture.

Tailor Toyo

This men's reversible embroidered souvenir jacket is made in China and produced by Tailor Toyo, Toyo Enterprises' label specializing in reproductions of vintage Japanese souvenir jackets, commonly known as sukajan. Based on an early-1950s-style Japanese souvenir jacket, this model combines a fully reversible two-face construction with 100% acetate satin on both sides, contrast raglan sleeves, striped rib-knit trim, slanted double-welt pockets, a vintage-style metal zipper, and embroidery that evokes the character of period examples. The construction, materials, embroidery character, color blocking, and deliberately vintage-oriented surface appearance reflect the historical souvenir-jacket tradition inherited by Tailor Toyo from Kosho & Co., the predecessor of Toyo Enterprises. Combining authentic vintage-inspired character, bold visual appeal, and practical everyday wearability, the jacket offers a distinctive yet versatile addition to a contemporary casual wardrobe.

Tailor Toyo and the Japanese Souvenir-Jacket Tradition:
- Souvenir jackets, commonly known in Japan as sukajan, developed after World War II as commemorative garments for American servicemen stationed in Japan. Jackets were embroidered with East Asian motifs such as eagles, tigers, dragons, Mt. Fuji, and cherry blossoms, as well as place names, military-unit references, and other imagery associated with the servicemen's time in Japan.

- Kosho & Co., the predecessor of Toyo Enterprises, was involved in the production and supply of souvenir jackets during the early postwar period and played an important role in the development of this type of garment. Tailor Toyo is Toyo Enterprises' sukajan label and continues the history and tradition associated with those early Japanese souvenir jackets.

Early-1950s-Style Design:
- This model takes its design inspiration from vintage sukajan of the early 1950s. It reproduces characteristic elements found on period examples, including acetate satin fabric, contrast raglan sleeves, striped rib-knit trim, welt pockets, and embroidery intended to evoke the character of vintage souvenir jackets.

- The jacket is fully reversible. The eagle side and tiger side each have their own color arrangement, embroidery, pockets, and sleeve decoration, allowing either side to be worn as the exterior.

100% Acetate Satin on Both Sides:
- Both sides of the jacket are constructed from 100% acetate satin. The fabric has a silk-like luster, but rather than producing a harsh mirror-like shine, its appearance changes subtly according to the viewing angle and the way light falls across the surface.

- The acetate satin is relatively lightweight and supple. Natural wrinkles and drape develop as the fabric moves with the body, giving the jacket the fluid character associated with vintage acetate souvenir jackets.

Vintage-Oriented Fabric Character:
- The satin is finished to reproduce characteristics found on vintage sukajan fabrics, including subtle weave irregularities, natural wrinkles, and slight surface waviness. Fine wrinkles and variations in reflected light may therefore be visible even when the garment is new.

- These characteristics are intentional aspects of the fabric and are intended to reproduce the material character of older acetate souvenir jackets rather than the perfectly uniform surface of modern formal satin.

Unpadded Lightweight Construction:
- This jacket contains no insulating fill. The body is constructed from the two layers of acetate satin that form the reversible sides, with no batting, pile, or other insulating material placed between them.

- As a result, the jacket does not have the thickness or bulk associated with padded sukajan and has a comparatively lightweight feel. It can be worn over a T-shirt, shirt, lightweight sweatshirt, or similar inner layer as a lightweight outer jacket.

Fully Reversible Construction:
- The jacket is designed to be worn from either side. The reverse face is not simply a conventional lining with added embroidery. Each side has its own color arrangement, embroidery, hand pockets, and sleeve decoration.

- Because the colors and motifs differ substantially between the two sides, each face presents a distinctly different appearance while sharing the same underlying jacket construction.

Front Zipper Closure:
- The front uses a full-length zipper closure. The metal zipper pull is engraved with "T.Y.E." and "TOKYO."

- The zipper is constructed for the reversible design so that the jacket can be opened and closed regardless of which side is being worn as the exterior.

Raglan Sleeve Construction:
- The sleeves use raglan construction. Diagonal seams extend from the neckline toward the underarm to join the sleeves to the body.

- This construction eliminates conventional shoulder seams and creates a continuous line from the shoulder into the upper arm. The diagonal raglan seams also emphasize the contrasting sleeve panels and decorative sleeve lines characteristic of sukajan construction.

Striped Rib-Knit Trim:
- The collar, cuffs, and waistband are made from 100% acrylic rib knit. Each rib-knit section is folded into a double-layer construction and attached to the satin body. The elasticity provides a moderate degree of fit around the neck, wrists, and hem.

- Contrasting stripes are knitted into the rib trim and coordinate with the color combinations used on the two reversible satin faces.

Rib-Knit Collar:
- The neckline is finished with a striped rib-knit collar. The elastic knit follows the neck and forms the characteristic neckline associated with classic sukajan.

Rib-Knit Waistband:
- A striped rib-knit waistband is attached around the lower body. Its elasticity gently draws in the hem while retaining moderate room through the body.

Rib-Knit Cuffs:
- Matching striped rib knit is also used at the sleeve cuffs. The elasticity gently reduces the sleeve opening so that the satin sleeves narrow naturally toward the wrists.

Slanted Double-Welt Hand Pockets:
- Both sides of the reversible jacket have slanted hand pockets at the waist. Each pocket opening is finished with contrasting double welts.

- Small triangular reinforcement pieces are attached at the ends of the openings. The combination of narrow welt construction and triangular reinforcement is a characteristic pocket detail found on many vintage sukajan.

Rayon Embroidery:
- The embroidered areas are worked with rayon thread. The characteristic luster of rayon reflects light differently from the acetate satin background, giving the outlines and individual embroidered motifs a degree of visual depth.

- Changes in stitch direction also affect the way light is reflected, allowing areas of the same thread color to appear lighter or darker depending on the viewing angle.

Vintage-Style Embroidery Character:
- The embroidery is designed to reproduce the visual character found on vintage sukajan. Rather than creating completely uniform outlines and stitch density, variations in stitch direction, density, outlines, and overlapping threads contribute to a less mechanically uniform appearance and a softer sense of depth.

- Because the embroidery places localized tension on the lightweight satin, fine wrinkles or puckering may appear around embroidered areas. These characteristics are also part of the vintage-oriented appearance of the jacket.

Eagle Side:
- The front side combines a black body with ivory raglan sleeves. Eagle embroidery is positioned on both sides of the chest, facing toward the center, while the back features a large eagle with its wings spread against a pine-tree motif.

- Script-style "Japan" lettering is embroidered above the back design, recalling the Japanese origin traditionally represented on postwar souvenir jackets.

Eagle-Side Raglan Sleeve Detail:
- The ivory raglan sleeves feature tape-like lines in the same black color as the body. Rope-style piping is inserted along the edges of these lines.

- The combination of contrasting panels and raised rope-style piping reproduces the decorative sleeve treatment seen on vintage sukajan.

Tiger Side:
- The reverse side combines a blue body with black raglan sleeves. Tiger-head embroidery is positioned on both sides of the chest, facing toward the center, while a large tiger motif forms the principal embroidery on the back.

- The blue body and black sleeves create a distinctly different color arrangement from the black-and-ivory eagle side.

Tiger-Side Raglan Sleeve Detail:
- The black raglan sleeves feature tape-like blue contrast lines that coordinate with the blue body.

- Unlike the rope-style piping used on the eagle side, the reverse side relies primarily on the contrasting blue sleeve lines for its decorative treatment.

Overall Construction and Design:
- Tailor Toyo Lot No. TT15972-119 combines a fully reversible 100% acetate satin construction with contrast raglan sleeves, striped acrylic rib-knit trim, slanted double-welt hand pockets, rayon embroidery, and a reversible metal zipper.

- The black-and-ivory side features eagle imagery, while the blue-and-black reverse side features tiger imagery. The different color combinations, embroidery motifs, and sleeve treatments allow the two faces to present distinctly different appearances within the same lightweight, unpadded sukajan construction.

Model Name:

TOYS McCOY Men's Plain Two-Tone Crew Neck Sweatshirt, 14.8 oz. Extra-Heavyweight Brushed-Back Cotton, Tubular Body, Unwashed, Made in Japan (TMC2670)

TOYS McCOY

Available Colors

This men's long-sleeve crew neck sweatshirt is made in Japan by TOYS McCOY and is based on the functional construction and proportions of early 20th-century American athletic wear and vintage sweatshirts. It is constructed from substantial 14.8-ounce extra-heavyweight 100% cotton sweatshirt fabric with a brushed interior and features a tubular side-seam-free body, a binder-finished crew neck, double-layer V-gussets at both the front and back neckline, long set-in sleeves, extended rib-knit cuffs and waistband, and four-needle flatseam construction. Contrasting rib-knit sections are used at the neckline, V-gussets, cuffs, and bottom hem to create a classic two-tone appearance, while the exposed flatseam stitching emphasizes the garment's construction and adds subtle visual definition. With no printed graphics or embroidery, the sweatshirt relies on its heavyweight fabric, traditional construction, rib proportions, and stitching details to create an authentic vintage-inspired character. At the same time, its clean design and balanced proportions make it easy to incorporate into contemporary casual outfits, whether worn on its own or layered under a jacket or coat.

Size and Fit Guide:

This item uses Japanese tagged sizing. Because the proportions may differ from typical U.S./EU sizing, please use the actual garment measurements below as your primary reference when selecting a size.

This sweatshirt is cut in a classic fit inspired by early American athletic wear and vintage crew neck sweatshirts. It has moderate room through the chest and body, combined with a relatively short body length. The shoulders are not cut excessively wide, and the set-in sleeve construction allows the sweatshirt to sit naturally around the shoulders while maintaining comfortable room through the chest and torso. The overall fit is not intentionally oversized or excessively loose.

The body falls naturally from the chest toward the waist without pronounced tapering. At the bottom, the wide, extended rib-knit waistband gently draws the sweatshirt in around the waist. This allows a small amount of the heavyweight body fabric to gather naturally above the waistband, creating the softly rounded silhouette associated with classic vintage sweatshirts. The extended rib-knit cuffs provide a secure, comfortable fit around the wrists and help control the volume of the sleeves.

The substantial 14.8-ounce extra-heavyweight fabric has enough thickness and body to help the sweatshirt maintain its shape rather than draping loosely against the body. This gives the garment a substantial vintage-inspired appearance while keeping the overall silhouette balanced and controlled. The relatively short body length also works well for classic layering, helping prevent the sweatshirt hem from extending too far below many jackets and coats.
